Q: I am exporting ~500,000 rows from MySQL into an XLSX file using batch processing A:

It would be better to edit the closed question and ask to reopen it instead of opening a new question.

Your first question can be answered as you still don't tell us what Excel library you use. You even forgot to tell us what programming language you use.

Third question: Excel is a spreadsheet application not a database. Therefore IMHO you should only use it if you need the data in that format. But as you don't tell us what you want to do in the end we can't answer your question no matter how often you create a new question on the same topic.

Q: Moving a file in C A:

I did not test what I am going to say. But I believe at least one of these techniques would work:

  1. I believe the system("" "") function works by executing bash in linux and CMD in Windows. So you could use the copy command from CMD and then delete the old file.

  2. You open the file in binary (works for everything but if its just test you can simply open it as normal "r"). Then you could write it somewhere else and finally you can delete the old file.

Q: How to programmatically detect if a path is a ZFS snapshot? A:

Based on comments on the question, and the Claude AI session linked to by @ChristophRackwitz, I have devised a solution which appears to work.

Claude's suggestion directly does not work; it suggests calling the libzfs function zfs_path_to_zhandle, and then calling zfs_get_type on the resulting handle. In theory, this can return ZFS_TYPE_SNAPSHOT. However, zfs_get_type does not return ZFS_TYPE_SNAPSHOT if zfs_path_to_zhandle is called with the path to a snapshot, only if zfs_path_to_zhandle given the object name of the snapshot and explicitly told to open a ZFS_TYPE_SNAPSHOT object.

But, looking at the source code to zfs_path_to_zhandle in the ZFS source code and combining findings there with what else is known about ZFS snapshot paths, including the fact that stat will return a different st_dev for the snapshot (also highlighted by Claude), I came up with a solution.

It starts with the heuristic that all paths that are contained in a ZFS snapshot will contain the components /.zfs/snapshot/. This, however, is not enough to detect with certainty that the path actually is contained in a snapshot. For instance, the user could simply create directories by these names. But, with some additional checks, I believe it is possible to eliminate the edge cases and come up with a confident result.

  1. The path might be a relative path. The rest of the processing depends upon it being a normalized full path. The system call realpath can expand a relative path to a full absolute path, collapsing . and .. components and duplicate / characters along the way.

  2. The path might refer to a symbolic link. Unfortunately, realpath always follows symbolic links, so if you want to be able to check paths to symlinks themselves (I do), then the realpath logic must be reimplemented. This is annoying, but is a SMOP. I haven't done this in the proof of concept linked to below but it doesn't require any further elaboration.

  3. Paths which do not contain the substring /.zfs/snapshot/ require no further processing. They are not contained in ZFS snapshots.

  4. The prefix leading up to this substring must be a ZFS mount point. The libzfs function zfs_path_to_zhandle, in its implementation, uses a function getextmntent which is provided on Linux by libspl. I use the same function and then check both the mnt_fstype and mnt_mountp members (the latter since getextmntent will find the mount point also for child paths contained within the mount point).

  5. The stat function returns a value st_dev that identifies the underlying device containing the path. The st_dev values for the mount point, ./.zfs and ./.zfs/snapshot within the mount point should all be the same. But, the st_dev value for ./.zfs/snapshot/SnapshotName (the path including just the first path component within the tail following the /.zfs/snapshot/ components) within the mount point should differ.

All of this is done in a loop, since the path could contain multiple instances of /.zfs/snapshot/, and there might be one that is legitimate that isn't the first one in the string.

I don't believe it is possible for a path to satisfy these criteria and not be contained within a ZFS snapshot.

/code/zfs_snapshot_test$ ./probe `realpath probe` /.zfs/snapshot/testsnapshot/code/zfs_snapshot_test/probe
/code/zfs_snapshot_test/probe: not in snapshot
/.zfs/snapshot/testsnapshot/code/zfs_snapshot_test/probe: in snapshot
/code/zfs_snapshot_test$

Source code: https://github.com/logiclrd/zfs_snapshot_test

Claude AI discussion from @ChristophRackwitz: https://claude.ai/share/630f8cda-7a24-46aa-a0ef-ae743cf51f40

(My proof of concept is in C, but I need C#, and so I will subsequently be reworking this to a proper C# implementation for use in DQD.RealTimeBackup.)

Q: Not wanted extension in File download A:

According to chatty

This happens because the server is serving the GPX file with an XML-related MIME type (like application/xml), so the browser assumes the correct extension is .xml and appends it automatically; the fix is to explicitly force the filename and extension by sending a proper Content-Disposition header such as Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="file.gpx" (and ideally Content-Type: application/gpx+xml) so the browser downloads it with the correct .gpx name instead of defaulting to .xml.
